title: Keva and Kavanah: A Rule of Life
hook: the last stretch is about living it: a short daily rule you choose yourself
carry: keva keeps the time, kavanah keeps the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the later voices with Moses at the back of Akiva's class, comforted. Add your voice. The last stretch of this year starts now, and it's about living it.

A notes-app list titled this year, with a goal for every part of life. A few weeks later it's a list of things you aren't doing. So the last stretch of this path tries something smaller: a rule of three lines, chosen by you. One thing in the morning, one in the day, one at night. Short enough to keep on a bad Tuesday. But can a rule that small hold a whole life? And should a spiritual life have rules at all? Jewish tradition has argued about exactly that.
screen: `A GOAL FOR EVERYTHING.` → `MORNING, DAY, NIGHT.` → `SHOULD A SPIRITUAL LIFE HAVE RULES?`

segments.voice: Here are both sides, each in its own voice. The first is Shammai, in Pirkei Avot: make your Torah study keva, fixed. A set time, every day, whether you feel like it or not. The case for it is simple. Feelings come and go; a fixed time is still there on the day the feeling isn't. A rule carries you through the gray weeks, and often the feeling comes back while you're keeping it. The second is Rabbi Shimon, also in Pirkei Avot: when you pray, don't make your prayer keva. Don't let it go rote, the same words rattled off like a grocery list. Make it a real plea, said with kavanah, intention, meaning it. The case for that is just as strong. A rule kept on autopilot can turn into the thing itself, and the heart quietly leaves the room. The Talmud even asks what keva means, and gives more than one answer: anyone whose prayer feels like a burden; anyone who doesn't say it as a plea; anyone who can't add anything new to it. Notice that the two aren't really enemies. Shammai is talking about protecting a time; Rabbi Shimon is talking about protecting the heart inside it. The tradition keeps both: the siddur gives fixed words at fixed times, and the sages keep asking whether you meant them. So a rule of three lines can hold a life, if you keep it fixed and keep asking.
